The TESS All-Sky Rotation Survey: Periods for 944,056 Stars Within 500 pcFacilities: TESS [82], Gaia [37, 38], Kepler [8], K2 [47], ZTF [6]

Abstract

Stellar rotation is a fundamental tracer of stellar magnetic evolution, age, and activity, with broad implications for Galactic archaeology and exoplanet characterization. The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) provides high-precision time-series photometry across the sky, enabling rotation measurements for an unprecedented number of stars. We present the TESS All-Sky Rotation Survey (TARS), an all-sky catalog of stellar variability periods for 944,056 stars with T<16T<16 and distances within 500 pc. We estimate that 94% of these periods are rotation periods. This catalog increases the number of rotation period measurements for stars with T<16T<16 within 100 pc by a factor of 2.1 and within 500 pc by 3.7. We also present a method to correct half-period aliases in TESS data and show that it reliably recovers periods as long as 25 days from a single TESS sector. TARS represents the largest homogeneous catalog of stellar rotation periods to date, providing a foundation for studies of stellar ages, young associations, and Galactic structure. We make the light curves used in our analysis available as a HLSP through MAST11 1 https://archive.stsci.edu/hlsp/tars. Beyond the default TARS catalog, we provide code that allows users to generate rotation period catalogs with adjustable completeness and reliability thresholds. This code and all rotation period measurements are available through Zenodo22 2 10.5281/zenodo.18342590.

I Introduction

Stellar rotation is a key observable that traces the magnetic and structural evolution of low-mass stars. Young stars form with a wide range of rotation periods [79] and spin up as they contract toward the zero-age main sequence. Stars with convective envelopes subsequently undergo magnetized-wind braking that steadily removes their rotational angular momentum [87, 101, 92]. These processes link surface rotation to stellar age, magnetic activity, and internal structure, making rotation periods essential diagnostics across the main sequence.

In exoplanet science, stellar rotation presents both opportunities and challenges. Since stellar rotation encodes the ages of main-sequence stars [4, 11], it provides a path toward studying exoplanet evolution over time. This is most relevant for evolutionary processes that alter planets over the first billion years [71, 24, 96, 58, e.g.,]. A key observational challenge, however, is that the transit and radial velocity methods are biased against active stars. The community has developed creative approaches to this issue for both transits [52, 83, 45, 39] and radial velocities [17, 55, 5, 25], enabling progress despite these challenges.

Over the past decade, wide-field photometric surveys have enabled rotation measurements for tens of thousands of stars. Kepler established that the rotation distribution of field K and M dwarfs is bimodal, both in the Kepler field [63] and across the ecliptic [81]. Ground-based studies have measured rotation periods for nearby stars [7, 51], open clusters [36, 31], and M dwarfs [65, 61].

The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite [82, TESS;] provides a unique opportunity to build on these previous studies. TESS provides high-quality photometry for nearly every star with T≲16T\lesssim 16 across the sky, enabling rotation measurements over a sample that no previous survey could approach. Although the 27-day observing window of a single sector limits sensitivity to periods beyond ≃12\simeq 12 days, TESS is still sensitive to the fast and moderate rotators that dominate young populations, and there has been some success extending this 12-day barrier [19, 43]. Crucially, TESS’s all-sky footprint allows rotation to be mapped across Galactic environments rather than restricted to individual fields or clusters.

This all-sky capability has already begun to reshape our understanding of stellar populations [21, 56, 102]. For example, Boyle et al. [12] used TESS rotation periods and Gaia astrometry to show that the Pleiades is part of a much larger complex of associated stars. Such studies illustrate the crucial role of all-sky rotational catalogs.

To date, no existing study has produced a flux- and distance-limited catalog of TESS rotation periods. Previous TESS rotation efforts have focused on specific clusters [67, 29, 93] and known planet hosts [18, 94]. Broader studies by Fetherolf et al. [34] and Colman et al. [20] have used two-minute data from the TESS prime mission to identify tens of thousands of new variable stars. However, most stars within 500 pc of the Sun have not been observed by TESS at two-minute cadence due to the heterogeneous nature of the two-minute data product [33]. In contrast, the TESS full-frame images (FFIs) offer an opportunity to homogeneously survey the local neighborhood for stellar variability.

In this paper, we present the TESS All-Sky Rotation Survey (TARS): an all-sky catalog of rotation periods for stars within 500 pc with T<16T<16. We emphasize transparent selection functions and provide multiple catalog layers that allow users to trade completeness against reliability depending on their needs. We aim to provide a community resource that not only reports TESS rotation periods but also maps reliability and completeness across the sky. This enables all-sky studies of stellar ages, young associations, and Galactic structure, and supports improved exoplanet characterization through reliable rotation constraints.

II Target Selection

We aim to measure reliable stellar rotation periods for as large and diverse a sample as possible. Our selection function is therefore guided by three considerations: (1) maximizing the number of stars with measurable rotation periods, (2) ensuring that TESS has sufficient photometric sensitivity to recover those periods, and (3) achieving broad coverage of nearby, known stellar associations to use as validation benchmarks. Given these considerations, we chose to focus on stars observed by TESS with T<16T<16 and d<500d<500 pc. We constructed the resulting target list as follows.

  1. 1.

    We began with stars in TIC v8.2 [72] satisfying T<16T<16 and Gaia DR2 ϖ>2\varpi>2 mas. This initial cut yielded 7,914,103 stars.

  2. 2.

    We removed sources flagged as duplicates in TIC v8.2, eliminating 127,205 stars.

  3. 3.

    We excluded stars lacking an associated Gaia DR2 source identifier in the TIC, removing 986 stars.

  4. 4.

    For the remaining targets, we identified corresponding Gaia DR3 sources using the Gaia DR3 dr2_dr3_neighbourhood table. We required matches within 2​″2\arcsec and a magnitude difference Δ​G<0.5\Delta G<0.5 mag. When multiple candidate matches satisfied these criteria, we adopted the DR3 source with the smallest angular separation. The cross-matched sample contained 7,710,873 stars.

  5. 5.

    We removed stars with missing Gaia DR3 GG, B​PBP, or R​PRP photometry, yielding 7,655,488 stars.

  6. 6.

    We then used tess-point [15] to determine whether each star fell on TESS silicon. This process yielded 7,481,412 stars observed by TESS at least once between Sectors 1–96 (2018 July–2025 September).

We adopted this final set of 7,481,412 stars as our target sample. We show general information about these targets in Figure 1. Our selection function includes 97% of AFGK dwarfs out to 500 pc, and a similar fraction of partially-convective M dwarfs out to ≃\simeq250 pc. Most targets have multiple sectors of data, corresponding to a total of 39,061,674 star–sector observations.

For this sample, we corrected the photometry for interstellar extinction and computed effective temperatures (TeffT_{\rm eff}) following Boyle et al. [12]. In brief, this procedure involved combining the three-dimensional dust maps from Vergely et al. [99] with the Gaia DR3 extinction coefficients from Fitzpatrick et al. [35]. We then estimated effective temperatures (TeffT_{\rm eff}) using an updated version of the Gaia DR2 color–TeffT_{\rm eff} relation from Curtis et al. [23], recalibrated for Gaia DR3 photometry.

III Generating Light Curves

This work is focused on measuring rotation periods for stars brighter than T<16T<16 within 500 pc. Given the available TESS data products at the time of our analysis, the best match for our needs was the full-frame images. While a wide variety of data processing efforts have yielded TESS light curves [53, 64, 9, 48, 16, 41, 42], the selection functions of these analyses and their availability through MAST did not match our requirements.

The unpopular package [44] enables light curve extraction from FFIs and has a proven track record in studies of stellar rotation [12, 43, 93, e.g.,]. To remove TESS systematics, unpopular uses a causal pixel model [100], which assumes that signals common to many pixels within an image are instrumental, while signals unique to individual pixels are astrophysical. A systematics model is constructed from these shared signals and removed from each target light curve. The package is open-source33 3 https://github.com/soichiro-hattori/unpopular and straightforward to deploy, making it well suited for large-scale surveys. We used the unpopular version corresponding to Git commit 5653498.

We used unpopular following the same setup as in Boyle et al. [13]. Briefly, for each star and sector, we used TESSCut to extract a 50×5050\times 50 pixel cutout from the calibrated FFIs centered on the target coordinates. Prior to systematics correction, we subtracted a background estimated from the median counts of the 300 faintest pixels in each image. We then constructed a systematics model using light curves from 100 pixels of similar brightness, excluding all pixels within 5 pixels of the target. unpopular prevents overfitting by using a regularization parameter (λ\lambda) that constrains the model flexibility, which we set to 0.1. We then divided each light curve into 100 temporal segments, trained the systematics model on each of the other segments, and applied the resulting best-fit coefficients to the holdout segment. Subtracting this model yielded the final corrected light curve for each star.

We applied this procedure to all 39,061,674 star–sector combinations in our survey, yielding one light curve for each star in each sector in which it was observed.

IV Methods

IV.1 Measuring Periodic Signals

For each of our 39,061,674 light curves, we used a Lomb-Scargle (LS) periodogram [59, 86] as implemented in astropy (​​Astropy Collaboration et al. 3, Astropy Collaboration et al. 1, Astropy Collaboration et al. 2) to search for periodicity. The details of our implementation and all parameters we recorded are given in Appendix A. This procedure returned 39,044,567 non-null periodogram measurements (17,107 were null). These measurements can be accessed and downloaded from Zenodo44 4 10.5281/zenodo.18342590. Figure 2 shows an example light curve and periodogram. Similar plots for all rotation measurements in the TARS survey are available at MAST55 5 https://archive.stsci.edu/hlsp/tars.

IV.2 Vetting Periodic Signals

The best-fit frequency in a Lomb-Scargle periodogram corresponds to the strongest sinusoidal signal in the light curve, but this signal does not necessarily correspond to stellar variability. In particular, instrumental systematics—including momentum dumps and scattered light—can produce prominent periodic signals. In addition, Kepler revealed numerous FGK stars with rotation periods of 20-30 days [63]. While the amplitudes of such signals might be detected by TESS, the periods themselves are usually resolved as the half-period harmonic.

We addressed the issues of systematics classification and alias identification using two sequential random forest classifiers. Random forest classifiers have previously been shown to perform well in identifying stellar rotation periods [85, 84, 14], and behave well for large datasets. We designed our first classifier (hereafter: the systematics classifier) to separate instrumental systematics from rotation signals. We trained the second classifier (hereafter: the alias classifier) to separate half-period aliases from accurately-measured rotation signals. We describe each in detail below.

IV.2.1 The Systematics Classifier

The most common systematics in TESS light curves are scattered light from the Earth and Moon, and spacecraft momentum dumps. The average TESS light curve therefore has excess power at harmonics of the spacecraft orbital period, and at harmonics of the time interval between momentum dumps (Figure 3). Prior work has taken advantage of this period-clustering to remove non-astrophysical systematics [34]. Signal amplitudes offer an independent dimension to separate signal from noise. Our approach, beyond recording Lomb-Scargle peak periods and the amplitudes of the associated best-fit Fourier models, is to compute a few dozen light curve and periodogram features (see Appendix A), and to use them as inputs for our systematics classifier.

We trained the systematics classifier using two labeled samples: a set of rotation period measurements that we deemed reliable (the positive class) and a set that were dominated by systematics (the negative class). We opted to define our positive and negative classes using internal consistency across multiple TESS sectors. For the positive class, we selected stars observed in five or more TESS sectors for which the measured rotation period agreed across all sectors within 3​σ3\sigma, with uncertainties from Equation 1 of Boyle et al. [13]. For the negative class, we selected stars also observed in five or more sectors but for which the inferred rotation periods were inconsistent between every sector. These measurements were therefore more likely to be systematics or noise than true rotational modulation. This procedure yielded 508,455 measurements in the positive class (persistent signals) and 1,490,169 measurements in the negative class (inconsistent signals). To balance the training data, we randomly drew from the negative class to match the size of the positive class.

We implemented a random forest classifier using sklearn’s RandomForestClassifier with 100 estimators, reserving 20% of the data for validation [75]. We show classifier performance and feature importance diagnostics in Appendix B. The results were insensitive to the number of estimators and other hyperparameter variations, so we adopted the default settings. To guide feature selection, we introduced a control variable constructed by randomly permuting the measured Lomb-Scargle peak-power values among stars, and computed its feature importance. All adopted features had higher importance than this randomized control.

For the rest of this paper and in our plots, we refer to measurements with a high probability from this classifier of being an astrophysical signal as having a high P⁡(signal)P(\rm signal). Measurements with a high probability of being a systematic have a high P⁡(systematic)P(\rm systematic). Since this is a binary classification problem, these quantities are related by P⁡(systematic)=1−P⁡(signal)P(\mathrm{systematic})=1-P(\mathrm{signal}).

When evaluated on the validation set, the classifier correctly identifies 99% of the negative class and 98% of the positive class. The corresponding false positive and false negative rates are 0.9% and 2%, respectively. As an additional performance metric, we compute the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), where an AUC of 0.5 indicates no predictive power and an AUC of 1 corresponds to a perfect classifier. Our classifier achieves an AUC of 0.998, indicating excellent performance. The overall accuracy (the proportion of all classifications that are correct), precision (the proportion of periods classified as reliable that are actually reliable), and recall (the proportion of reliable periods classified as reliable) scores were 98.54%, 99.11%, and 97.95%, respectively. As shown in Appendix B, the classifier relies most strongly on the signal-to-noise ratios of the first five periodogram peaks, the amplitude of the best-fitting sinusoid, and the width of the highest periodogram peak.

The effectiveness of the classifier is visually apparent in the bottom-left panel of Figure 3. Using Sector 6 as an illustrative example, the low-probability points coincide with systematic-driven overdensities, where the vertical streak at ∼3\sim 3 days is from momentum dumps. We highlight this with two specific examples in the bottom-right panel of Figure 3. The top light curve, with a systematics classifier score of 1.0, exhibits clear, coherent rotational modulation that is readily identifiable by eye. The lower example, with a low probability (0.0), shows low-amplitude variability that is ambiguous and difficult to confidently attribute to stellar rotation. Visual inspection of similar systems suggests the classifier is effectively separating out rotation from systematics.

Defining the Signal Detection Threshold: While we provide the means for anyone to select a rotation catalog optimized for their science (see Section VIII), we need to adopt a threshold for the standard data product. We also need to quantify the role a shifting detection threshold has on the sample. To this end, we employ a mix of (1) reliability and completeness diagnostics, and (2) manual vetting.

Following Boyle et al. [13], we define reliability as the fraction of stars the systematics classifier correctly identifies as being in each class and completeness as the fraction of signals in each class that are successfully recovered. Figure 4 illustrates the tradeoff between reliability and completeness for the systematics classifier. Reliability remains high even down to a P⁡(signal)>0.5P(\mathrm{signal})>0.5, with a slight drop-off at the longest periods for thresholds <<0.7. Completeness remains high for periods ≲10\lesssim 10 days, but declines at longer periods due to the duration of TESS single-sector observations.

We manually vetted a randomly selected sample of ∼4,000\sim 4{,}000 measurements. For each, we visually inspected the TESS light curve, the light curve phase-folded at the period corresponding to the highest Lomb-Scargle peak, and the periodogram itself. We found that periods associated with a systematics classifier threshold ≳0.8\gtrsim 0.8 were generally convincing, while measurements with 0.5<P⁡(signal)<0.80.5<P(\mathrm{signal})<0.8 were often ambiguous and difficult to assess with confidence. Periods with P⁡(signal)<0.5P(\mathrm{signal})<0.5 were rarely judged to be reliable.

Based on the combined evidence from the reliability and completeness analysis (Figure 4) and the manual vetting, we required that a measurement have a systematics classifier threshold P⁡(signal)>0.8P(\mathrm{signal})>0.8 to pass this stage of vetting. Applying this cut to our hold out validation sample, we find that 99.69% of the measurements that pass this threshold are reliable and we still capture 96.29% of reliable detections.

IV.2.2 The Alias Classifier

While the systematics classifier is effective at separating instrumental systematics from astrophysical variability, it does not identify period aliasing incurred by the TESS window function. To address this issue, we trained a second random forest classifier to identify harmonics of the true period—most commonly Prot/2P_{\rm rot}/2. Since this is a binary classification problem with matches defined as the positive class and aliases defined as the negative class, a high probability from the alias classifier is a high probability that the measured period is a match, whereas a low probability indicates that the measured period is an alias.

For the alias classifier, we defined positive and negative training classes using the Kepler rotation period catalog of McQuillan et al. [63] (hereafter M14). Kepler’s four-year observing baseline and 95 cm aperture yielded rotation periods that are well-suited to identifying period aliases. M14 reported 34,030 rotation periods spanning 0.2–70 days out of a parent sample of 133,030 stars. We generated TESS light curves for this sample as in Section III. Starting from the 34,030 stars with detected periods in M14, we determined which targets were observed by TESS using tess-point, and excluded stars that were not observed, lacked valid Gaia DR3 photometry, or had T>16T>16. This yielded 312,860 TESS light curves corresponding to 32,684 unique stars. We then computed Lomb–Scargle periodograms and recorded the same set of parameters described in Appendix A.

For each sector, we compared our measured period to the corresponding M14 period. We classified a measurement as a match if the periods agreed within 3​σ3\sigma, as defined by Equation 1 of Boyle et al. [13], and as an alias if the measured period agreed within 3​σ3\sigma with half of the M14 period. To mirror our full vetting pipeline, we then applied the systematics classifier described in Section IV.2.1 to this sample. A total of 47,708 measurements satisfied our quality cut of P⁡(signal)>0.8P(\mathrm{signal})>0.8, of which 34,513 were matches and 13,195 were aliases. To balance the training data for the alias classifier, we then randomly selected 13,195 measurements from the matched sample.

We again reserved 20% of the data as a hold-out validation set and used K-Fold cross-validation to train the random forest model. We used sklearn’s RandomForestClassifier with n_estimators = 200, max_features = 0.5, and criterion = entropy. We left the rest of the values at their default sklearn values. We list the adopted features in Appendix A, and their importances in Appendix B.

Our alias classifier distinguishes true rotation periods from aliases with high fidelity. It correctly identifies true rotation signals in 89% of cases and correctly flags aliases in 85% of cases. Aliases are incorrectly classified as true signals 11% of the time (the false-positive rate), and true rotation periods are misclassified as aliases in 15% of cases (the false-negative rate). The discriminative performance of the classifier is strong, with an AUC of 0.951. The resulting classification achieves an accuracy of 87.3%, with a precision of 85.9% and a recall of 89.3%. Among the input features, the difference in BIC between a two-term Lomb–Scargle model evaluated at the period of the highest periodogram peak and at twice that period provided the greatest discriminatory power. Other important features included the ratio of the first and second detected periods, the Lomb–Scargle power evaluated at twice the best period, and the period corresponding to the second-highest Lomb–Scargle peak.

Defining the Alias Detection Threshold: Figure 5 illustrates how reliability and completeness vary as a function of P⁡(alias)P({\rm alias}) for the alias classifier. For all tested thresholds, the minimum reliability exceeds 80% at all periods. Adopting a stringent threshold (e.g., a probability >0.9>0.9 of being the true rotation signal) ensures that more than 90% of the selected periods are not aliases, independent of rotation period. The corresponding completeness, shown in the right panel, highlights the cost of such a cut: requiring a threshold >0.9>0.9 would remove up to half of the potential matches from the sample. These trends are summarized in Table 1 and provide a quantitative guide to those who wish to adjust these settings (see Section VIII).

Adopted Detection Thresholds: Based on Figures 4 and 5, we adopted a probability threshold of 0.8 for both matches and aliases. While this removes 30-35% of rotation period detections, it ensures that >96%>96\% of our reported periods are the true rotation signal and not an alias.

IV.3 Period Adoption Logic

The default TARS periods are intended to balance reliability and completeness. A user might be interested in a catalog that is more reliable but less complete, or vice versa. Our Zenodo66 6 10.5281/zenodo.18342590 contains code and suggestions for how to take our catalog and make different period selections based on science needs. We built our standard rotation period catalog as follows:

  1. 1.

    Sector-level periods. We began with the highest-power Lomb–Scargle peak (see Section IV.1) from the light curve for each sector of every target.

  2. 2.

    Period metrics. For each sector of every target, we computed the metrics listed in Appendix A.

  3. 3.

    Apply systematics classifier. We removed any sector-level periods with P⁡(signal)<0.8P(\rm signal)<0.8 (Section IV.2.1).

  4. 4.

    Flag half-period aliases. We flagged all targets with a P⁡(alias)>0.8P(\rm alias)>0.8 as likely aliases and targets with a P⁡(match)>0.8P(\rm match)>0.8 as likely matches.

  5. 5.

    Alias corrections. We doubled the measured periods of all sector periods flagged in the previous step as being aliases.

  6. 6.

    Propagate alias corrections to consistent sectors. We doubled any other sector-level periods for a flagged target (i.e., at least one sector was flagged as an alias), provided the period was within 15% of the undoubled period.

  7. 7.

    Assign uncertainties. We assigned each period an uncertainty using Equation 1 of [13].

  8. 8.

    Consistency check against the doubled-period ensemble. We computed a weighted mean of the doubled periods (if any exist). Sector measurements that were not doubled were retained as-is, and those that agreed with the doubled-period weighted mean to within 15% were treated as consistent with the corrected period in subsequent averaging.

  9. 9.

    Outlier rejection. We applied 3​σ3\sigma-clipping (with the median absolute deviation as the scatter estimator) to the set of periods to remove discrepant sector-level measurements.

  10. 10.

    Compute the adopted period. The adopted rotation period was then the weighted mean of the clipped periods. Our uncertainty was the standard error on the weighted mean.

This procedure ensures that exactly one final rotation period was adopted for each star, while explicitly accounting for aliasing, inter-sector consistency, and measurement uncertainty. This yielded a catalog of 944,056 stars with adopted period measurements. We show the structure of this catalog in Table 2.

IV.4 Quality Flagging

We created a series of quality flags that can be used to isolate the highest-quality period detections from the catalog above. The name of the flag is followed by its parameter name in Table 2:

  1. i)

    Binary flag (flag_possible_binary) — Boolean flag set True for a target if any sector used to calculate the adopted period shows a non-harmonic peak (not within 10% of n​PbestnP_{\rm best} or Pbest/nP_{\rm best}/n for n≤5n\leq 5) that has power greater than a fixed threshold (default power = 0.2). It will also be set to True if the Gaia RUWE >1.4>1.4 or non_single_star>0>0.

  2. ii)

    Bad coverage flag (flag_bad_coverage) — Boolean flag for insufficient temporal coverage relative to the inferred period. Observation times are split into groups separated by gaps larger than 0.1 d; the durations of these groups are summed to give an effective coverage window. The flag is set True if this window is less than the period corresponding to the highest peak in the periodogram.

  3. iii)

    Multiple-period flag (flag_multiple_periods) — Boolean flag set to True if any sector period used to calculate the final, adopted period lies more than 10% away from the adopted period and its first-order harmonics (ProtP_{\rm rot}, 2​Prot2P_{\rm rot}, or Prot/2P_{\rm rot}/2), indicating potential residual multi-period behavior.

  4. iv)

    Doubled period flag (flag_doubled_period) — Boolean flag set to True if any of the sector-level periods involved in calculating the adopted period were doubled.

  5. v)

    Contamination flag (final_n_contams) — A nearby star could reproduce the observed variability amplitude (AobsA_{\rm obs}) if its variability amplitude (AreqA_{\rm req}) is at least

    Areq=Aobs​(100.4​Δ​G+1).A_{\rm req}=A_{\rm obs}\,\left(10^{0.4\,\Delta G}+1\right). (1)

    We use Δ​G\Delta G as a proxy for Δ​T\Delta T since not all stars needed for this calculation are in the TIC. We assign a maximum plausible intrinsic amplitude (AmaxA_{\rm max}) for a neighbor, taken to be the 95th percentile of the best fit amplitudes from stars with similar GBP−GRPG_{\rm BP}-G_{\rm RP} colors as the neighbor. Any star with Amax>AreqA_{\rm max}>A_{\rm req} is taken to be a potential contaminant. The contamination flag is the number of such contaminants within 1​′1\arcmin radius (approximately three TESS pixels) of the target in Gaia DR3. Since the variability amplitude varies between sectors, we first calculate the number of potential contaminants in each sector, then report the minimum number of contaminants across sectors used to calculate the final period.

If we were to require no possible binaries, no multiple-periods, and no potential contaminating neighbor stars (final_n_contams = 0), we would have a catalog of 313,916 periods. Additionally requiring the period to be measured in multiple TESS sectors would yield a catalog of 202,223 rotation periods. Based on literature comparisons, these periods are considered the highest quality, but users may readily construct alternative samples or apply their own set of flags based on their science case (see Section VIII for instructions).

V Validation with Literature Periods

To validate our rotation period measurements, we compare our derived periods against four independent samples with well-established rotation periods: Kepler, K2, ZTF, and an open cluster compilation. Our primary goal is to quantify how the reliability and completeness of our catalog depend on user-defined probability thresholds and quality-flag selections, and to provide guidance on how these choices affect the final sample.

For each dataset, we first consider the simplistic baseline yielded by adopting the highest peak in the Lomb–Scargle periodogram as the rotation period for peaks with Lomb–Scargle power exceeding 0.05. For this baseline, we also apply the period-adoption logic from Section IV.3, but without the systematics or alias classifier. We then compare this baseline against the periods yielded by various classifier thresholds to explore the costs and benefits of our random forest classification.

V.1 Kepler

For the Kepler validation, we calculate our statistics on the holdout validation sample from Section IV.2.2 and use stars with T<16T<16 and Prot<40P_{\rm rot}<40 days. This yields a comparison sample of 60,699 sector-level measurements for 27,711 stars. We process the TESS data for these stars through the same pipeline applied to our TESS targets, including both the systematics (Section IV.2.1) and alias classifiers (Section IV.2.2) with varying random forest probability thresholds. For a given threshold (RF=X{\rm RF}=X), we require that each sector-level measurement passes the systematics and alias classifier (true period or true alias) with the same probability (>X>X). After adopting a final rotation period following Section IV.3, we compare it to the Kepler period. We repeat this procedure for X=X= 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, and 0.9.

We also consider two quality-flagging regimes: one in which no quality flags (see Section IV.4) are applied and another in which all of our quality flags are enforced (the highest-quality periods). The results are summarized in Table 3, which reports both the number of recovered stars and the fraction of matches, half-period aliases, double-period aliases, and non-recoveries.

In the baseline case with no quality flags applied, only 44.7% of the adopted periods match the Kepler periods, with a substantial fraction (20.8%) identified as half-period aliases. Applying all quality flags improves reliability: the match fraction increases to 68.8%, albeit at the cost of completeness, with periods recovered for ∼3%\sim 3\% of the validation sample.

A similar tradeoff is observed when varying the classifier probability thresholds. Without quality flags, increasing the threshold from 0.5 to 0.9 raises the match fraction from 60.6% to 83.5%. When all quality flags are applied, the corresponding match fractions increase from 77.5% to 92.2%. In all cases, higher thresholds suppress aliases but reduce the total number of retained stars.

In terms of alias contamination, the half-period alias rate decreases from 20.8% in the un-flagged baseline sample to just 0.0% when adopting strict probability thresholds (>0.9>0.9) and applying all quality flags. For users seeking an especially clean sample, requiring a threshold >0.9>0.9 from both the systematics and alias classifiers (i.e. the probability that a period is the true period >0.9>0.9) provides a clean sample. Under these criteria, and with all quality flags applied, we recover 564 Kepler stars with match, half-alias, double-alias, and non-recovery fractions of 0.922, 0.000, 0.007, and 0.071, respectively. Without quality flags, the same selection yields 3,661 stars with corresponding fractions of 0.835, 0.018, 0.021, and 0.126.

V.2 K2

We perform an analogous validation using rotation periods measured from the K2 mission. For our K2 comparison sample, we take the rotation period measurements from Reinhold and Hekker [81] with Prot<40P_{\rm rot}<40 days and require Hpeak>0.3H_{\rm peak}>0.3. After cross-matching with our full target list, we are left with 16,823 stars in common. As for the Kepler validation, we process these stars through the full TARS pipeline and adopt final periods using the same logic described in Section IV.3.

For the baseline comparison, only 35.6% of the adopted periods match the published K2 periods, with a large fraction (32.9%) identified as half-period aliases (Table 3). This highlights the prevalence of aliasing in K2 light curves when no additional vetting is applied.

Applying the random forest classifiers substantially improves the reliability of the recovered periods. Without quality flagging, increasing the probability threshold from 0.5 to 0.9 raises the match fraction from 68.5% to 87.8%, while reducing the half-period alias rate from 9.4% to 3.7%. When all quality flags are enforced, the match fraction improves further, reaching 94.0% at a threshold of 0.9, with a corresponding half-period alias rate of 1.1%. As expected, these gains in reliability come at the cost of completeness: the number of recovered stars decreases from 1,319 in the baseline flagged sample to 799 at the most stringent threshold.

These results are shown visually in the middle row of Figure 6. The trends mirror those seen for Kepler: the vast majority of stars that pass our vetting agree with the K2 period, with ∼4%\sim 4\% of the remaining measurements being inadvertently doubled. As in the Kepler case, our alias flagging and period-doubling logic enables recovery of rotation periods beyond what is typically achievable in a standard single-sector TESS light curve.

V.3 ZTF

For the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) comparison, we adopt rotation periods from Lu et al. [61]. After cross-matching with our target list, we obtain a validation sample of 18,894 stars that satisfy our selection criteria.

In the baseline case with no quality flags applied, 80.7% of the adopted periods match the ZTF literature values, with 7.6% identified as half-period aliases and 11.3% classified as non-recoveries (Table 3). Applying all quality flags increases the match fraction to 93.5%, demonstrating that our periods are generally consistent with ZTF-derived period measurements.

Increasing the random forest probability threshold further improves reliability. Without quality flags, the match fraction rises from 71.7% at a threshold of 0.5 to 94.6% at a threshold of 0.9. When all quality flags are enforced, the match fraction increases from 80.3% to 97.3% over the same range, while the half-period alias rate decreases to 0.1%. As in the other validation samples, these gains come at the cost of completeness, with the number of recovered stars decreasing from 4,774 in the baseline flagged sample to 3,187 at the most stringent threshold.

The ZTF validation results are shown in the bottom row of Figure 6. Compared to Kepler and K2, ZTF exhibits a lower baseline alias rate and higher overall agreement, likely due to the ZTF sample being dominated by M dwarfs that inherently have higher rotation amplitudes. Nevertheless, the same reliability–completeness tradeoffs apply, and the TARS framework provides a consistent and flexible means of selecting rotation samples with well-quantified purity across space-based and ground-based surveys.

V.4 Open Clusters

Cluster membership provides an independent and physically motivated benchmark, as stars of similar age are expected to occupy coherent loci in rotation–effective temperature space. We adopt rotation periods for eight open clusters from Long et al. [60] that are well-represented in our survey: Taurus (4 Myr), ρ\rho Ophiuchus (9 Myr), Upper Scorpius (19 Myr), the Pleiades (123 Myr), NGC 1750 (316 Myr), Praesepe (741 Myr), the Hyades (758 Myr), and NGC 6774 (2.9 Gyr). Together, these clusters span nearly three orders of magnitude in age, providing a complementary validation sample to the Kepler, K2, and ZTF comparisons presented above.

This cluster validation sample contains 2,632 stars that satisfy our selection criteria. As above, we process these stars through the full TARS pipeline and evaluate recovery statistics as a function of random forest probability threshold and quality-flag selection.

In the baseline case with no quality flags applied, 72.7% of the adopted periods match the literature values, with 9.1% identified as half-period aliases and 16.9% classified as non-recoveries (Table 3). Compared to the field-star samples, the baseline cluster match fraction is substantially higher, reflecting the coherence of cluster rotation sequences and the higher-quality light curves available for many of these targets.

Applying increasingly stringent probability thresholds improves the match fraction in a manner similar to the Kepler and K2 samples. Without quality flags, the match fraction increases from 70.8% at a threshold of 0.5 to 89.6% at a threshold of 0.9. When all quality flags are applied, the match fraction rises from 75.8% to 94.8% over the same threshold range. Selecting stars with P⁡(signal)>0.9P(\rm signal)>0.9 and P⁡(match)>0.9P(\rm match)>0.9 or P⁡(alias)>0.9P(\rm alias)>0.9 almost entirely eliminates half-period aliases, reducing their incidence to 0.0%0.0\%. As before, these improvements in reliability are accompanied by a reduction in completeness, with the number of retained stars decreasing from 599 in the baseline flagged sample to 466 at the most stringent threshold.

VI Results

VI.1 Overall Catalog Properties

The TARS catalog provides period estimates for 944,056 stars within 500 pc. If we apply our suggested quality cuts (Section IV.4) to remove potential contaminants, targets with evidence of multi-period behavior, likely binaries, and stars that share a period with a nearby star, we have a ‘clean’ sample of 313,916 stars. Of these, 202,223 stars constitute our highest-quality subset, possessing consistent period measurements across multiple TESS sectors. We show the distribution of the 944,056 star sample as a function of period, amplitude and effective temperature in Figure 7. We examine structure in these diagrams in the discussion (Section VII) below.

Our default catalog reports rotation periods for 44,580 stars with T<16T<16 and d<100d<100 pc. To assess how many of these periods are newly measured, we cross-matched our target list against a set of previously published rotation period catalogs. For each catalog, we list the number of matches with T<16T<16 and d<100d<100 pc, along with the corresponding instrument used to measure the rotation periods: Kounkel et al. [56] (TESS; 1,782 stars), Fetherolf et al. [34] (TESS; 12,632), Schochet et al. [88] (ASAS-SN; 1,000), Lu et al. [61] (ZTF; 2,419), Holcomb et al. [46] (TESS; 4,670), Colman et al. [20] (TESS; 3,454), Claytor et al. [19] (TESS; 685), Reinhold and Hekker [81] (K2; 1,094), McQuillan et al. [63] (Kepler; 103), Oelkers et al. [68] (KELT; 5,233), Newton et al. [65] (MEarth; 230), Newton et al. [66] (MEarth; 188), Long et al. [60] (Kepler and K2; 211), Jayasinghe et al. [51] (ASAS-SN; 850), Van-Lane et al. [97] (multiple instruments; 159), and Distefano et al. [28] (Gaia DR3; 1,867). Together, these sources provide prior period measurements for 27,437 stars in the T<16T<16, d<100d<100 pc sample. Our catalog contains 30,301 stars with T<16T<16 and d<100d<100 pc that do not have reported periods in the above catalogs. Our catalog therefore increases the number of bright stars with known rotation periods within 100 pc by a factor of 2.1. Applying the same calculation out to 500 pc yields an increase by a factor of 3.7. The spatial distribution of the catalog viewed top-down in Galactocentric coordinates is shown in Figure 9, where selecting fast rotators enhances the visibility of young stellar associations.

VI.2 Overall Reliability of the TARS catalog

The validation tests presented in Section V imply that the default TARS catalog is reliable across a wide range of stellar populations. When adopting our default thresholds (systematics and alias classifier probabilities >0.8>0.8) without imposing additional quality flags, the recovered rotation periods agree with independent literature measurements at the ∼\sim85–90% level, depending on the comparison sample. Agreement is highest for ZTF and open clusters, where baseline match fractions exceed 80%, and somewhat lower for the Kepler and K2 samples, which are more susceptible to half-period aliasing in the absence of our additional vetting. Averaged over all validation sets and accounting for the relative sample sizes, we estimate that approximately ∼85%\sim 85\% of the periods in the default catalog correspond to the true stellar period, ∼5%\sim 5\% half-period aliases, ∼5%\sim 5\% double-period aliases, and ∼5%\sim 5\% blends or contamination from nearby stars.

When requiring multi-sector agreement, good temporal coverage, no evidence of binarity or multi-period behavior, and no plausible contaminating neighbors, the resulting subset exhibits match fractions of ≳85%\gtrsim 85\% across all validation samples, reaching ≳90%\gtrsim 90\% for open clusters and ZTF and ∼89%\sim 89\% for Kepler. Under these stricter criteria, we estimate that ∼92%\sim 92\% of these measurements reflect the true rotation period. Residual contamination is dominated by a small fraction of doubled periods rather than half-period aliases, and the incidence of non-matches is correspondingly low.

We took the additional step of inspecting some of the non-matches across the various samples. Using the Kepler 0.8 threshold with quality flags on from Table 3, we find 63 stars where our measurement did not agree with the Kepler measurement. After visually examining these measurements, we find that our measurements typically agree with the periodic signal present in our light curves. For the ∼9%\sim 9\% non-match rate in the Kepler validation sample, we find that 76%76\% of this contamination comes from stars with adopted periods of less than one day.

One explanation for the poorer Kepler recovery is blending or contamination: the median distance to the stars with rotation periods that were not recovered in the Kepler sample is 886 pc, compared to 579 pc for the stars with rotation periods that were recovered. Comparatively, the median distance to both the matches and non-recoveries in the K2 sample is ∼190\sim 190 pc. For a fixed angular resolution (the 21″ TESS pixel), the probability of a background source contaminating the aperture increases with the distance probed through the Galactic disk. Furthermore, the Kepler field’s relatively low Galactic latitude (b≃13​degb\simeq 13\deg) results in a higher integrated background stellar density. This increased crowding both dilutes the signal from the primary and risks introducing other periodic signals from nearby stars, including those with amplitudes exceeding those captured by our contamination flag (e.g., eclipsing binaries). Indeed, when we manually inspected the difference images (rotation peak-trough) of the TESS pixel files, many were centered on an adjacent pixel. Fortunately, this does not seem to be an issue for the main catalog as the stars are much closer (d<500d<500 pc) and spread over the whole sky.

Overall, these results show that the reliability of the TARS catalog is both high and tunable. Users interested in maximizing sample size can work with the default catalog while accepting a modest level of contamination, whereas users requiring highly secure rotation periods — such as gyrochronology calibration, cluster membership analysis, or detailed comparisons to stellar evolution models — can readily isolate subsets of the data with reliability approaching that of space-based long-baseline surveys.

VI.3 Effectiveness of Alias-Flagging

The effectiveness of our alias-flagging procedure is illustrated in Figure 8. In this figure, we cross match membership lists for the Pleiades, Praesepe, and the Hyades from Hunt and Reffert [49] with the default TARS catalog with quality flags applied. For reference, we show literature K2 rotation sequences for the Pleiades [78], for Praesepe [77], and for the Hyades [30].

In the left column, measurements flagged as aliases with P⁡(alias)>0.8P(\rm alias)>0.8 are shown in yellow, literature periods in gray, and measurements flagged as matches with P⁡(match)>0.8P(\rm match)>0.8 are in green. At higher effective temperatures our recovered periods closely follow the literature sequence. Toward cooler temperatures and longer periods, an increasing fraction of recovered periods fall systematically below the literature sequence, forming a distinct lower sequence that is characteristic of half-period aliases. This is especially true for Praesepe and the Hyades.

Most stars on these lower sequences are flagged by our alias classifier. The right panel shows the recovered rotation sequences after applying our doubling logic. In particular, this procedure recovers the slow-rotator sequence at periods ≳13\gtrsim 13 days, which is often assumed to be challenging to measure reliably from single-sector TESS observations. The cost is that a small number of stars were incorrectly identified as aliases, pushing them well above the sequence. This can be mitigated by adjusting the alias classifier threshold, at the cost of losing some correctly-classified periods (Table 3).

Table 3 shows that the completeness for clusters in our default catalog should be ∼65%\sim 65\%. An independent test of this estimate follows from noting that 735 Hyads from Hunt and Reffert [49] overlap with the TARS target list, and 454 of these stars appear in our default catalog. These counts suggest a completeness of 62%, in close alignment with the expected value. Praesepe is further away (d∼190d\sim 190 pc compared to ∼50\sim 50 pc for the Hyades), implying a more challenging test case. Hunt and Reffert [49] lists 803 Praesepe members that overlap with the default TARS catalog and 364 appear in the default catalog, implying a completeness of 45%.

VI.4 Additional types of variability

The TARS catalog reveals significant structure in TeffT_{\rm eff} and MGM_{G} space, as we show in Figures 7 and 10. The Kraft break [57] is apparent as a jump in the density of points and a change in the variability amplitude behavior around TeffT_{\rm eff}≳6600\gtrsim 6600 K.

The population of short-period variables above the Kraft break are unlikely to be from spots and stellar rotation. Instead, these are predominantly pulsators (e.g., δ\delta Scuti and γ\gamma Doradus) or other kinds of variables recovered by the Lomb-Scargle periodogram.

Populations of sub-giants and giants are also visible in the base catalog. These land well above the main-sequence with TeffT_{\rm eff} generally between 4000 K and 6000 K. This population mostly vanishes in the high-quality catalog, however, most of the surviving targets land in or near the instability strip. Like those above the Kraft break, these are more likely to be pulsations or other sources of variability than spots and rotation.

To estimate the fraction of our measured periods that correspond to rotational modulation, we cross-matched the default TARS catalog with the Gaia DR3 vari_classifier_result table, which contains the variability classifications from Gaia DR3 [32]. This cross-match returned 287,752 sources. Of these, 226,060 are classified as Solar-like modulation, 32,285 as RS CVn systems, 10,047 as young stellar objects (YSOs), 9,702 as eclipsing binaries, 7,092 as δ\delta Scuti, γ\gamma Doradus, or SX Phoenicis pulsators, and 1,861 as chemically peculiar Ap/Bp stars. The locations of these variability classes in rotation–temperature and color–magnitude space are shown in Figure 10.

Assuming the Gaia DR3 classifications are correct and that the detected periods for Solar-like stars, RS CVn systems, YSOs, and Ap/Bp stars arise from rotational modulation, we find that approximately 94% of the matched sample corresponds to stellar rotation. We adopt this value as an empirical estimate of the fraction of rotation periods in our catalog.

VI.5 Unresolved Binaries

Stars that appear brighter than the single-star main sequence on a color–magnitude diagram are likely to be spatially unresolved binaries. This effect is evident in the top panels of Figure 10, where a narrow overdensity above the main sequence is the binary sequence.

Simonian et al. [91] quantified this effect in the Kepler rotator sample of McQuillan et al. [63], defining a photometric binary as a star lying more than 0.3 mag above the main sequence. They found that 59% of fast rotators (1.5≤Prot<71.5\leq P_{\rm rot}<7 days) met this criterion, compared to 29% across the full sample, suggesting that most fast rotators are not young single stars, but are instead tidally synchronized binaries.

Here, we perform a similar analysis to estimate the photometric binary fraction in our sample. We begin by selecting a high-purity sample of rotators from the TARS catalog. We adopt stars with P⁡(signal)P(\rm signal), P⁡(match)P(\rm match), and P⁡(alias)>0.8P(\rm alias)>0.8, enforce all quality cuts, and remove alias periods rather than doubling them. These steps yield match rates exceeding 95% across validation sets.

To define the single-star main sequence, we bin stars in MG,0M_{G,0}–TeffT_{\rm eff} space (using 60 bins), and compute the 70th percentile of MG,0M_{G,0} in each bin. This choice prioritizes stars on the lower envelope of the CMD—fainter at fixed TeffT_{\rm eff} and thus more likely to be single. A spline fit to these percentile points defines the empirical main-sequence locus for 4500<Teff<65004500<T_{\rm eff}<6500 K, avoiding cooler stars where the binary sequence blends with young single-star populations [54]. The result is shown in Figure 12(a) as the red curve.

We define the photometric excess as:

Δ​MG=MG,0−MG,locus,\Delta M_{G}=M_{G,0}-M_{G,\mathrm{locus}}, (2)

where MG,0M_{G,0} is the dereddened absolute magnitude and MG,locusM_{G,\mathrm{locus}} is the expected magnitude for a single star at that TeffT_{\rm eff}.

The distribution of Δ​MG\Delta M_{G} for stars in the cleaned sample with 4500<Teff<65004500<T_{\rm eff}<6500 K is shown in panel (b) of Figure 12. The binary sequence peaks near Δ​MG∼−0.75\Delta M_{G}\sim-0.75, consistent with equal-mass binaries.

Adopting the threshold Δ​MG<−0.3\Delta M_{G}<-0.3 to identify photometric binaries, we find that 25.2% of stars in our sample meet this criterion, comparable to the 28% reported by Simonian et al. [91]. Panel (c) shows that the binary fraction is strongly dependent on rotation period, exceeding 45% among the fastest rotators and declining to ∼5%\sim 5\% at longer periods. This provides additional evidence for the correlation between binarity and rapid rotation. Panel (d) shows the TeffT_{\rm eff}–ProtP_{\rm rot} distribution after removing stars with Δ​MG<−0.3\Delta M_{G}<-0.3.

VI.6 Structure in ProtP_{\rm rot}–TeffT_{\rm eff} Diagram

The observed density of stars in the ProtP_{\rm rot}–TeffT_{\rm eff} plane encodes at least three separate effects: (1) the underlying stellar age distribution; (2) the mapping from age to rotation period and variability amplitude, including the effects of binarity; and (3) the survey’s selection function, including both detection efficiency and biases in period recovery.

The middle panel of Figure 13 shows the number density of TARS detections in the ProtP_{\rm rot}–TeffT_{\rm eff} plane. The morphology is complex, with many over- and under-dense regions. We discuss the most important regions below, and connect them to the median rotational amplitudes shown in the lower panel.

VI.6.1 Non-Astrophysical Effects Near Harmonics of TESS Orbital Period

The top and middle panels of Figure 13 show under-dense regions near Prot≈6.8P_{\rm rot}\approx 6.8 and 13.613.6 days, and over-dense regions near 10 and 20 days. The under-dense regions align with harmonics of the lunar-month timescale of the TESS orbit. We believe at least three effects contribute to these over- and under-dense regions. First, in low-amplitude light curves, gap-related systematics can masquerade as periodic signals (Figure 3). Our systematics classifier rejects such signals, as most are not astrophysical. However, the systematics classifier could be overly aggressive, due to the high density of real systematics. Second, our alias classifier struggles to differentiate between matches and aliases in the 6-8 day gap (see the top right panel of Figure 5). The incompleteness of the alias classifier in these regions contributes to the under-densities. Finally, our measured periods near harmonics of the TESS orbital period suffer ≲\lesssim5% biases, revealed by the slight non-linearities in Figure 6. These tend to move stars from under- to over-dense regions, particularly near the 10 day and 20 day peaks. We note that the incidence of non-recovered periods from our validation samples is <10%<10\% through these overdensities, which suggests that most of the recovered periods in the overdensities are reliable.

VI.6.2 Astrophysical Period Gap Spanning F8V-M2V

Cool Star Gap Recovered: The “intermediate period gap” in the rotation period distribution for K and M dwarfs has been documented in numerous studies of Kepler, K2, and ZTF data [63, 26, 81, 40, 27, 61, e.g.,]. At Teff≲5000T_{\rm eff}\lesssim 5000\,K, Figures 11 and 13 show that the TARS sample recovers this gap, and is most similar in stellar density to the Kepler and K2 samples.

Two possible explanations for the cool star gap have been previously discussed. The first is that the gap coincides with a decrease in photometric variability amplitude [80, 81], which would reduce the detectability of rotation periods. In this first scenario, the physical origin of the amplitude decrease could be linked to the transition from spot- to faculae-dominated rotational modulation [90, e.g.,]. The alternative explanation invokes a phase of accelerated spin-down following core-envelope recoupling, during which stars rapidly evolve through intermediate rotation periods [22, 40, 61]. The intermediate period gap identified in our sample coincides with a region of systematically lower variability amplitudes (Figure 7), consistent with both interpretations.

The Gap Extends to Sun-like Stars: The number density of K0V-F8V (5300-6200 K) stars at ≲\lesssim10 days in Figure 13 shows a diagonal underdensity: for TESS, these (roughly) Sun-like stars separate into a cool and a hot branch. This underdensity appears to be an extension of the now-classic Kepler and K2 “intermediate period gap” to hotter stars. The same region shows reduced photometric variability amplitudes in Figure 7 and the lower panel of Figure 13, as a diagonal blue swath between two higher-amplitude branches, continuously spanning temperatures of 3800-6200 K. While K2 previously showed local minima in variability amplitudes in this hotter region [81], the drop in apparent number density of stars is, to our knowledge, new to the TARS sample. Photometric binarity seems to not be related, since Figure 12d shows the same structure in a sample with photometric binaries removed. Our alias handling is also not related, since the same figure includes no period doubling.

Why does TESS see this underdensity for Sun-like stars, when Kepler and K2 did not? In ProtP_{\rm rot}-TeffT_{\rm eff}-amplitude space, the continuity of the diagonal low-amplitude gap implies a single physical cause, perhaps the spot- to faculae-dominated transition [80]. In ProtP_{\rm rot}-TeffT_{\rm eff}-number density, there are two key distinguishing factors when comparing TESS and Kepler/K2. The Kepler prime mission was biased against young stars since its average target was one scale height above the galactic plane, where kinematic heating lifts older stars [10]. TESS targets span all galactic latitudes, and so do not share this selection bias against young stars. Separately, Kepler and K2 were also more sensitive to lower-amplitude photometric modulation, which would tend to fill in regions with low number density. A quantitative reconstruction of the stellar age and number density distributions from TARS would be a worthy topic for future work. However, it is beyond our current scope.

VII Discussion

The TARS catalog is a search for periodic variability encompassing 7,481,412 stars observed in TESS Sectors 1–96 with T<16T<16 and distances d<500d<500 pc. With more than 900,000 period detections that pass our default selection, this catalog will be invaluable for a wide range of studies, including stellar spin-down, young associations, and stellar ages.

VII.1 Effectiveness of Doubling Aliases

A major benefit of our catalog is the extension to longer-periods thanks to our alias classifier. With this, we are able to extend TESS rotation studies to stellar populations and age regimes that were previously inaccessible due to TESS’s short observational baseline. This improvement is illustrated by the rotation sequences of Praesepe and the Hyades shown in Figure 8. After applying the alias correction, the full rotation sequences of both clusters are recovered, enabling the construction of coherent rotation sequences for older clusters using TESS data alone.

A similar effect can be seen in Figure 11, where the intermediate period gap for cool stars with long rotation periods (Prot≳13P_{\rm rot}\gtrsim 13 days) is also recovered. The presence and morphology of this gap closely match those seen in the Kepler, K2, and ZTF samples, all of which benefit from longer observational baselines and are therefore less susceptible to the aliasing issues that affect TESS.

The downside of the classifier is that it sometimes incorrectly doubles the period. We have made the decision to use the alias classifier to double half-period aliases (which can comprise up to ∼30%\sim 30\% of detections). This virtually eliminates half-period aliases but comes at the cost of ∼4%\sim 4\% of the sample being erroneously doubled. Alternative options for an interested user include using the code on Zenodo to remove aliases instead of doubling them, or manually inspecting the vetting plots (Figure 2).

VII.2 Areas For Caution

Several caveats should be kept in mind when interpreting the TARS catalog and the structure of the ProtP_{\rm rot}–TeffT_{\rm eff} plane. First, blending and residual contamination from neighboring stars can introduce spurious periods (Section IV.4), even when the star is multiple TESS pixels away from the target star [cf. 93, Figure 7]. Users interested in rotation periods for stars in crowded regions such as the galactic plane should take care to account for potential contamination.

Second, our alias-doubling strategy substantially reduces half-period contamination but introduces a small (∼\sim3–4%) residual population of incorrectly doubled periods (Section IV.2.2). In addition, mild period-recovery biases and harmonics of the TESS window function imprint under- and over-densities near ∼\sim6–8, ∼\sim10, and ∼\sim20 days (Section VI.6). While our validation samples show that the periods in these regions are reliable, users could take the additional step of manually vetting individual periods of interest, including by adopting their own for treating multi-sector information.

VII.3 Future Directions

Longer rotation periods. The present analysis derives rotation periods from individual TESS sectors. Recent studies [19, 43] have demonstrated that rotation periods up to ∼80\sim 80 days can be recovered in the TESS continuous viewing zones by combining multi-sector data. Extending TARS to incorporate multi-sector light curves would therefore enable the recovery of longer periods. A particularly promising avenue would be to adapt the methodology of Hattori et al. [43] to non-consecutive sectors, testing whether coherent long-period signals can be reconstructed even when observations are temporally separated. Because most TARS targets were observed in multiple sectors, such an extension could enable long-period measurements for a significant fraction of the sample.

Improved classification. Our alias classifier currently misidentifies ∼15%\sim 15\% of rotation periods as doubled periods without adopting a stricter P⁡(alias)P(\rm alias) or P⁡(match)P(\rm match) threshold, like we do in constructing our default catalog. This behavior suggests partial overlap between true matches and aliases in feature space, limiting separability. Developing additional or more discriminating features — particularly those sensitive to harmonic structure or phase coherence — could improve class separation and reduce systematic doubling errors. Refining the classifier would increase both completeness and reliability, especially for moderate-amplitude signals.

Variability classification. Although we estimate that ∼94%\sim 94\% of reported periods correspond to stellar rotation, we have not attempted to subdivide the catalog by variability type. Implementing a dedicated variability classifier (for example, an additional random forest trained to distinguish rotational modulation from pulsation, eclipses, or other variability) would produce a cleaner rotation-only subset. Such a classification would both enhance rotation-focused studies and facilitate investigations of non-rotational variability within the broader TARS sample.

VIII Conclusion

We have conducted an all-sky rotation survey with TESS by searching 7,481,412 unique stars for stellar variability across 39,061,674 TESS light curves. The main takeaways are as follows.

  1. 1.

    We have produced a catalog of 944,056 measured periods, ≈\approx94% of which are from stellar rotation. This expands the number of stars with known rotation periods by a factor of 2.1 within 100 pc and 3.7 within 500 pc. The most common types of other variability include eclipsing binaries, δ\delta Scuti pulsators, and γ\gamma Doradus pulsators.

  2. 2.

    Our methodology allows us to remove half-period aliases and recover reliable rotation periods as long as 25 days from a single TESS sector.

  3. 3.

    We provide a quantitative framework for evaluating the completeness and reliability of this catalog and show that our periods largely agree with rotation periods from Kepler, K2, and ZTF.

  4. 4.

    We recover the intermediate period gap for stars cooler than 5000 K with ProtP_{\rm rot}≥\geq13 days, matching the morphology seen in Kepler, K2, and ZTF. The detection of this gap in TESS data, facilitated by our alias-correction framework, demonstrates that TARS can be used to study the angular momentum evolution of stars well into their intermediate-age “stalled” spin-down phase.

  5. 5.

    We observe an extension of the intermediate period gap to hotter stars, which manifests as two separate ProtP_{\rm rot}-TeffT_{\rm eff} branches in the number density of K0V-F8V (5300-6200 K) stars at ≲\lesssim10 days. Both the hot and cool regions of the period gap overlap with a local minimum in rotation amplitudes, and so probably share a common origin.

  6. 6.

    We confirm a distinct transition in rotational behavior and variability amplitude near the Kraft break at TeffT_{\rm eff}≃6600\simeq 6600 K. This provides an empirical benchmark for the disappearance of deep convective envelopes in massive stars.

  7. 7.

    By analyzing the color-magnitude distribution of our rotators, we confirm that a significant portion of rapid field rotators (<7<7 d) are tidally synchronized binaries. The binary fraction among the fastest rotators exceeds 45%, compared to ≃5%\simeq 5\% for stars on the slow-rotator sequence.

We recognize that users may have different science needs and that the default catalog we present may not be sufficient for each science goal. To that end, we have written a command line utility that allows a user to rebuild our catalog based on the different systematics classifier, alias classifier, and quality flagging thresholds appropriate for their science. This script will also estimate completeness and reliability statistics for the user-defined inputs based on the same validation samples in Section V. This script is available on Zenodo77 7 10.5281/zenodo.18342590. Our light curves and vetting plots are available at MAST as a High Level Science Product88 8 https://archive.stsci.edu/hlsp/tars via 10.17909/2sff-fn29 (catalog 10.17909/2sff-fn29). Each of our 39 million sector level measurements are also available on Zenodo and follow the table format described in Appendix C.

Appendix A Lomb-Scargle Implementation and Calculated Parameters

We computed the Lomb Scargle periodogram using a linearly spaced grid in frequency from 0.1 to 20 days with one million points. This is over-sampled relative to the available Nyquist information content [98] but keeps gaps between grid points below the measurement uncertainties, even at the longest periods.

We pre-process our data by performing sigma clipping to remove points more than 3​σ3\sigma away from the median light curve value. This step removes outliers that could otherwise alter the results.

To model the dominant periodic signal, we fit both single- and two-term Lomb-Scargle models. The one-term Lomb-Scargle model captures simple sinusoidal variability and yields the amplitude, phase, and power of the best-fit sinusoid. However, stellar rotation signals often deviate from purely sinusoidal shapes. In such cases, a two-term model, which includes the first harmonic, can better describe non-sinusoidal light curve morphologies, such as double-dip modulations. The two term model is not used for our periodogram powers.

The full list of our recorded parameters is as follows:

  • •

    first_period, second_period, third_period, fourth_period, fifth_period: Periods (in days) of the top five Lomb–Scargle (LS) periodogram peaks after restricting to periods P<20​dP<20\,\mathrm{d} and enforcing each period to be >10%>10\% away from a previously recorded period. Periods greater than 20 days are only used for calculating the power at twice the period of the highest peak in the periodogram (see power_twice_period below).

  • •

    first_power, second_power, third_power, fourth_power, fifth_power: LS powers evaluated at the corresponding peak periods. The periodogram is computed on sigma-clipped fluxes and using a scalar flux uncertainty estimated from the point-to-point RMS (see p2p_rms).

  • •

    first_snr, second_snr, third_snr, fourth_snr, fifth_snr: A simple periodogram signal-to-noise-like metric for each peak, defined as the ratio of the peak power to the median power across the (full) computed periodogram: SNR≡powermedian⁡(power)\mathrm{SNR}\equiv\frac{\mathrm{power}}{\mathrm{median}(\mathrm{power})}.

  • •

    best_fit_amplitude: Amplitude of the best-fitting single-term LS model at the best frequency fbest=1/Pbestf_{\rm best}=1/P_{\rm best}. If the LS model parameters at fbestf_{\rm best} are 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} with sine and cosine coefficients θ1\theta_{1} and θ2\theta_{2}, the reported amplitude is A≡θ12+θ22A\equiv\sqrt{\theta_{1}^{2}+\theta_{2}^{2}}.

  • •

    time_first_minimum: Time of the first local minimum of the best-fitting LS model light curve, i.e., the earliest tt at which the model yfit​(t)y_{\rm fit}(t) has a local minimum. This is obtained by finding troughs in yfit​(t)y_{\rm fit}(t) and returning the time of the first such trough.

  • •

    first_peak_width: Width (in days) of the dominant LS peak in period space, measured at half-maximum using scipy.signal.peak_widths. Concretely, the width is computed in frequency space at half-height, converted to periods, and differenced: wP≡Pright−Pleftw_{P}\equiv P_{\rm right}-P_{\rm left}.

  • •

    p2p_rms: Point-to-point RMS noise proxy computed from successive flux differences Δ​Fj≡Fj−Fj+1\Delta F_{j}\equiv F_{j}-F_{j+1}. Let Δ​F~≡median⁡(Δ​F)\widetilde{\Delta F}\equiv\mathrm{median}(\Delta F) and define centered differences Δ​Fj′=Δ​Fj−Δ​F~\Delta F^{\prime}_{j}=\Delta F_{j}-\widetilde{\Delta F}. The reported value averages the upper and lower robust dispersions: p2p≡12​[(Q84−Q50)+(Q50−Q16)]\mathrm{p2p}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\left[(Q_{84}-Q_{50})+(Q_{50}-Q_{16})\right], where QpQ_{p} denotes the ppth percentile of the sorted Δ​Fj′\Delta F^{\prime}_{j} distribution.

  • •

    a_90_10: Flux amplitude defined as the 90th–10th percentile range of the fluxes: A90−10≡Q90​(F)−Q10​(F).A_{90-10}\equiv Q_{90}(F)-Q_{10}(F).

  • •

    red_chi2: Reduced chi-square of the best-fitting single-term LS model at fbestf_{\rm best}, using the point-to-point based scatter as the uncertainty scale. With residuals ri≡Fi−yfit​(ti)r_{i}\equiv F_{i}-y_{\rm fit}(t_{i}),

    χ2≡∑i=1N(rip2p​_​rms​(F))2,χν2≡χ2N−3,\chi^{2}\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\frac{r_{i}}{\mathrm{p2p\_rms}(F)}\right)^{2},\qquad\chi^{2}_{\nu}\equiv\frac{\chi^{2}}{N-3},

    where NN is the number of time points and N−3N-3 is the assumed number of degrees of freedom.

  • •

    snr: A heuristic signal-to-noise metric combining relative flux amplitude, noise, time baseline, and the inferred period:

    snr≡(A90−10p2p)​TbasePbest,\mathrm{snr}\equiv\left(\frac{A_{90-10}}{\mathrm{p2p}}\right)\sqrt{\frac{T_{\rm base}}{P_{\rm best}}},

    where Tbase≡max⁡(t)−min⁡(t)T_{\rm base}\equiv\max(t)-\min(t) is the time baseline and Pbest=first_periodP_{\rm best}=\texttt{first\_period}.

  • •

    power_twice_period: LS power evaluated at the frequency corresponding to twice the best period, i.e. at f=0.5​fbestf=0.5f_{\rm best} (equivalently, P=2​PbestP=2P_{\rm best}). The code finds the closest sampled frequency to 0.5/Pbest0.5/P_{\rm best} and records the power at that index.

  • •

    one_term_bic: Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) for the single-term sinusoidal model fit at fbestf_{\rm best}, computed as

    BIC1≡χ12+k1​ln⁡N,k1=3,\mathrm{BIC}_{1}\equiv\chi^{2}_{1}+k_{1}\ln N,\qquad k_{1}=3,

    with

    χ12≡∑i=1N(Fi−yfit​(ti))2σF2,\chi^{2}_{1}\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\left(F_{i}-y_{\rm fit}(t_{i})\right)^{2}}{\sigma_{F}^{2}},

    where σF≡p2p​_​rms​(F)\sigma_{F}\equiv\mathrm{p2p\_rms}(F) is treated as a per-point flux uncertainty.

  • •

    two_term_bic: BIC for a two-term (nterms=2n_{\rm terms}=2) LS model evaluated at half the best frequency (0.5​fbest0.5f_{\rm best}): BIC2≡χ22+k2​ln⁡N\mathrm{BIC}_{2}\equiv\chi^{2}_{2}+k_{2}\ln N, where χ22\chi^{2}_{2} is computed analogously using the two-term model prediction, and k2=5k_{2}=5 is the parameter penalty adopted in the code for nterms=2n_{\rm terms}=2.

  • •

    two_term_bic_same_period: Same as two_term_bic, but evaluating the two-term model at fbestf_{\rm best} (i.e. enforcing the same period as the primary peak).

  • •

    delta_bic: Difference in BIC between the two-term (at 0.5​fbest0.5f_{\rm best}) and one-term model: Δ​BIC≡BIC2−BIC1.\Delta\mathrm{BIC}\equiv\mathrm{BIC}_{2}-\mathrm{BIC}_{1}.

The following metrics are used only in the alias classifier:

  • •

    period_ratio_1_2: The ratio of first_period divided by second_period.

  • •

    period_ratio_1_3: The ratio of first_period divided by third_period.

  • •

    snr_ratio_1_2: The ratio of first_snr over second_snr.

  • •

    power_ratio_1_2: The ratio of first_power over second_power.
